topics.title: The basics of the language
topics.summary: The words you need before anything else: how to store a value, the types, how to make a choice, how to repeat something, and how to write a function.

lesson.heading: Storing a value: val and var
lesson.body:
A program works on values: a number, some text, a yes-or-no. To use one later you have to **put it somewhere and give that place a name**. Kotlin gives you two ways.

`val` creates something that is given a value once and never changes. `var` creates something you can give a new value to later.

The habit worth building: **start with `val` every time**, and switch to `var` only when you really have to change the value. A value that cannot change is one that cannot surprise you two hundred lines further down.

You do not have to say what kind of value it is: Kotlin works it out from what you wrote on the right of the `=`. That is **type inference**.

There is one distinction that catches everybody once. `val` freezes **the name**, not what is inside the thing it points to. A `val` holding a list means you cannot point it at a different list — but you can still add things to the list it already points to. If you want the contents frozen too, use a `listOf`, which has no way of adding anything.

lesson.heading: The types, and the conversions you have to write
lesson.body:
Four types cover nearly everything at the start. `Int` is a whole number, `Double` has a decimal point, `Boolean` is `true` or `false`, and `String` is text.

Two things behave differently from what people expect.

**Integer division throws away the remainder.** `7 / 2` is `3`, not `3.5`, because both sides are whole numbers so the answer is one too. If you want `3.5`, at least one side has to be a `Double`: `7 / 2.0`.

**Converting between number types has to be written out.** An `Int` does not become a `Long` on its own, even though no information would be lost. You write `n.toLong()`. It is deliberate: it makes the moment of conversion visible instead of hidden.

To put a value inside text you write `$name`, or `${...}` when it is more than a single name. That is **string templates**, and it is far more readable than gluing strings together with `+`.
lesson.code:
val a = 3              // Int
val b = 2.5            // Double

val n: Int = 3
val l: Long = n.toLong()   // written out: no silent conversion

println(7 / 2)         // 3   — two Ints, so the answer is an Int
println(7 / 2.0)       // 3.5 — one Double is enough

val name = "Ada"
println("Hello $name, you have ${2 + 3} messages")
// Hello Ada, you have 5 messages

lesson.heading: if and when give you back a value
lesson.body:
This is where Kotlin differs most from Java, and it is the first thing an interviewer checks.

**`if` is an expression**: it produces a value, so you can put it on the right of an `=`. There is no separate ternary `? :` operator in Kotlin, because `if` already does that job and reads better.

**`when` replaces `switch`**, and it does much more. It can match single values, several at once, ranges, types, or nothing at all — written with no argument it becomes a tidy chain of conditions. It stops at the first match, with no `break` anywhere.

The rule to remember: **when `when` is used as an expression, it must cover every case.** Either you list them all, or you add `else`. The compiler refuses otherwise, because a value has to come out and there would be nothing to produce. Used as a statement — where the result is thrown away — `else` is optional.

The nice consequence: with an `enum` or a `sealed` type, if you list every case you can leave `else` out, and then adding a new case makes the compiler point at every `when` you have to update.

lesson.heading: Repeating: loops and ranges
lesson.body:
`for` in Kotlin always walks through something: a range of numbers, a list, the letters of some text. There is no C-style `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)`.

Ranges have three forms, and mixing them up is the classic off-by-one:

`1..3` includes 3.
`1 until 3` stops at 2.
`3 downTo 1` counts backwards.

And `step` says how far to jump each time: `0..10 step 5` gives 0, 5, 10.

When you need both the position and the value, `withIndex()` hands you the pair. And when you just want to do something a fixed number of times, `repeat(3) { }` says so more clearly than a loop over a range you then ignore.

`while` and `do-while` exist and behave as you would expect, but you see them far less: `for` and `repeat` cover nearly everything.

lesson.heading: Writing a function
lesson.body:
A function is declared with `fun`: a name, the parameters with their types, and after the colon the type of what it hands back. If it hands nothing back, you leave that out — formally it returns `Unit`, which is Kotlin's way of saying "nothing useful".

If the whole body is a single expression, you can drop the braces and the `return` and write `= expression`. Most small functions are written that way.

Two features make calls much more readable:

**Default values.** A parameter can have one, and whoever calls can leave it out. One function with defaults replaces the four overloads you would have written in Java.

**Named arguments.** At the call site you can write `name = value`, which lets you skip the middle ones and, more importantly, makes `true` and `false` readable — `greet(shout = true)` says something, `greet(true)` says nothing.

The habit worth taking: **if a parameter is a `Boolean`, always name it at the call site.** Six months later it is the difference between understanding the line and having to go and look.
lesson.code:
fun sum(a: Int, b: Int): Int = a + b        // single expression: no braces

fun greet(name: String = "world", shout: Boolean = false): String {
    val text = "Hello $name"
    return if (shout) text.uppercase() else text
}

greet()                     // "Hello world"
greet("Ada")                // "Hello Ada"
greet(shout = true)         // "HELLO WORLD" — the first default is kept

fun log(msg: String) {      // no return type: it gives back Unit
    println(msg)
}

questions.prompt: What happens when you try to compile this?
questions.code:
val x = 10
x = 20
println(x)
questions.explanation: `val` means the name gets a value once and never again. The second line tries to give it another, and the compiler refuses. Nothing runs, so nothing is printed. With `var x = 10` it would work.
whyWrong: That would need `var`. With `val`, the second line never becomes part of the program.
Nothing is printed at all: compilation stops before there is anything to run.
A warning still produces a working program. This is an error, so there is no program.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
val a = 7
val b = 2
println(a / b)
questions.explanation: Both are `Int`, so Kotlin does whole-number division: it keeps the 3 and throws the rest away. For 3.5 one of the two has to be a `Double`, for instance `a / 2.0`.
whyWrong: 3.5 is what you get when a decimal number is involved. Here both are whole, so the answer is whole.
The remainder is thrown away, not rounded up. 3.5 becomes 3, never 4.
It compiles: dividing two `Int`s is perfectly normal. The surprise is in the result.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
val a = 2
val b = 3
println("$a + $b = ${a + b}")
questions.explanation: `$name` puts a value into the text, and `${...}` does the same for anything that has to be worked out first. So `a` and `b` become 2 and 3, and `${a + b}` is calculated and becomes 5. The `+` in the middle is just a plus sign in the text.
whyWrong: To print it literally you would have to escape the dollar sign, `\$a`. As written, `$` always starts a template.
What is inside `${...}` is worked out, not copied. That is the whole difference between the two forms.
It compiles: templates are the normal way of building text in Kotlin.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `1..3` includes 3, so you get 1, 2, 3. `1 until 3` leaves it out, so you get 1, 2. Read `until` as "up to, but not including".
whyWrong: They are the wrong way round: `..` is the one that includes the end.
They cannot both give the same, since one includes the last number and the other does not.
`1..3` stops at 3. There is no 4 anywhere.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
val a = 5
val b = 9
val max = if (a > b) a else b
println(max)
options: Error: in Kotlin if does not return a value
questions.explanation: In Kotlin `if` is an expression: it produces a value, so you can assign it. 5 is not greater than 9, so the `else` branch wins and `max` is 9. This is why Kotlin has no `? :` operator — it would be a second way of saying the same thing.
whyWrong: 5 would be the answer if the condition held. `a > b` is false.
`true` would be the value of the condition. What is assigned is one of the two branches.
It is exactly the opposite: `if` producing a value is one of the first things people notice about Kotlin.

questions.prompt: What happens when you compile this?
options: It does not compile: `else` is missing
questions.explanation: Here `when` is being used as an expression — its result is assigned — so it must produce a value for every possible input. `n` is an `Int` and the cases cover two of them, so the compiler demands an `else`. Used as a statement, with the result thrown away, `else` would be optional.
whyWrong: There is nothing to print: the program is never built.
Kotlin would have to invent a `null`, and for a `String` that is not even allowed. It refuses instead.
It fails at compile time, which is the point: the problem is caught before the program exists.

questions.prompt: What does this call print?
questions.code:
fun greet(name: String = "world", shout: Boolean = false): String =
    if (shout) "Hello $name".uppercase() else "Hello $name"

println(greet(shout = true))
options: Error: you cannot skip the first parameter
questions.explanation: Naming the argument lets you skip the ones before it: `name` keeps its default "world", and `shout` is true, so the text is upper-cased. This is also the readable way to pass a boolean — `greet(true)` would tell the reader nothing.
whyWrong: Lower case would mean `shout` was false. It is explicitly true here.
`true` goes into `shout`, not into `name`. That is exactly what naming it prevents.
You can skip them, as long as you name what comes after. That is why named arguments exist.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
val list = mutableListOf(1)
list.add(2)
println(list)
options: Error: list is a val, it cannot be changed
questions.explanation: `val` freezes the name, not what the thing it points to contains. You cannot point `list` at a different list, but you can add to the one it already points to. To freeze the contents too you would use `listOf`, which has no `add`.
whyWrong: The `add` really does run: the list afterwards holds two numbers.
That is the classic confusion. `val` is about the name; `mutableListOf` is about the contents.
Nothing is replaced: `add` puts a new element after the one already there.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code: println(Int.MAX_VALUE + 1)
questions.explanation: An `Int` has a fixed amount of room: from about minus two billion to plus two billion. Adding one to the largest value does not make it bigger — it wraps round to the smallest, like a car odometer rolling over. Nothing warns you, which is why you use `Long` when the numbers might get large.
whyWrong: That number simply does not fit in an `Int`. For it you would need a `Long`.
Kotlin does not check for overflow on `Int`: it wraps round silently. That is the dangerous part.
It compiles: there is nothing wrong with the syntax. The problem only appears in the result.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
val a = "kotlin"
val b = buildString { append("kot"); append("lin") }
println(a == b)
println(a === b)
questions.explanation: `==` asks "do they hold the same text?" — and they do, so `true`. `===` asks "are they literally the same object in memory?" — and they are not, because `b` was built at runtime while `a` is a literal the compiler put aside. Two different objects holding the same text.
whyWrong: They would only be the same object if Kotlin reused the literal, and a string built at runtime is not reused.
The contents really are identical, so `==` is true.
It is the wrong way round: contents equal, identity different.

topics.title: Null safety: the crash that does not happen
topics.summary: How Kotlin says "here there might be nothing", the four symbols you need, and the corners where a null can still get in.

lesson.heading: Two types where other languages have one
lesson.body:
The most common crash in Java is the `NullPointerException`: you call a method on something that is not there, and the program stops. The man who invented the idea of `null` later called it his "billion dollar mistake".

Kotlin removes it by splitting every type in two. `String` means **there is always text in here**. `String?`, with a question mark, means **there might be text, or there might be nothing**.

They are two different types, and the compiler will not let you mix them up. You cannot put `null` into a `String`, and you cannot call `.length` on a `String?` without first dealing with the possibility that there is nothing there.

The effect is that the crash moves from the running app to your screen while you are typing. The compiler stops you and says "this might be nothing, decide what to do". You cannot forget, because it does not let you.

The habit worth building: **make something nullable only when the absence actually means something**. A nullable type is a question the reader has to answer every time they see it, so it should be there for a reason.

lesson.heading: The four symbols
lesson.body:
Four pieces of syntax cover everything you do with nullable types, and they get used dozens of times in every file.

**`?.` — the safe call.** "Carry on only if there is something; if not, the whole thing is null." Useful for walking down a chain: `user?.address?.city`. As soon as one `?` appears, the result is nullable.

**`?:` — the Elvis operator.** "This, or if it is null, that." The name is a joke about the shape, turned sideways. The right-hand side can also be a `return` or a `throw`, which is what makes it so useful at the top of a function: either there is a value, or we leave.

**`!!` — "it is definitely there, and if not, crash".** This is you deliberately bringing back the Java crash. Sometimes right — something you yourself put there, which can only be missing if you made a mistake — but every `!!` is a promise. If you cannot explain in one sentence why it cannot be null, do not write it.

**`?.let { }`** — run this block only if there is something, and inside the block call it `it`. Handy when you need the value more than once.

lesson.heading: Smart casts, and where they stop working
lesson.body:
Kotlin is cleverer than it first appears. Once you have checked that something is not null, it **remembers** — inside that block you can use it as a normal non-null value, with no further ceremony. That is a **smart cast**.

It works for types too: after `if (x is String)`, inside the block `x` is a `String` and you can call string methods on it without writing a cast.

And there is one place it refuses, which produces one of the most puzzling error messages for beginners: **"smart cast is impossible, because the property is a mutable (var) property"**.

The reason is sound. If the property is a `var` belonging to another object, something else could change it between your check and your use — another thread, a method you call in between. The check would have been true and then stopped being true, and you would get exactly the crash Kotlin promised to prevent.

The fix is to copy it into a local `val` first. Then nobody can change it behind your back, and the smart cast works. Or use `?.let { }`, which does the same thing in one line.

lesson.heading: Where a null can still get in
lesson.body:
Kotlin's guarantee is strong, but it has one hole, and it is worth knowing exactly where.

When you call Java code, Kotlin usually cannot tell whether a value may be null — Java does not say. So it gives it a **platform type**, written `String!`, which means "I do not know". It is the one case where you are not protected: use it as non-null and it works, until one day it is null and you get the Java crash back.

What to do about it: when a value comes from Java, **declare the type yourself** on the Kotlin side. Write `String?` and deal with it, or `String` and accept that you are making a promise.

The same applies to things coming from outside the app in general: JSON from the network, a database column, a value from storage. Those are the places where reality disagrees with your types.

And one last oddity: string templates never crash. `"$x!"` with `x` null prints `null!`, because the template calls `toString()`, and that is defined to produce the text "null" rather than failing. Surprising the first time you see it, and occasionally the reason a user sees the word "null" in your interface.

lesson.heading: lateinit and lazy: two ways to arrive later
lesson.body:
Sometimes a value genuinely does not exist yet when the object is created, but it is not optional either — it will be there before anyone uses it. Making it nullable would mean writing `?` or `!!` on every single use, for a problem that only exists for a moment.

**`lateinit var`** is for that. "Non-null, but I will fill it in shortly." If somebody reads it before it has been set, you get a clear error that tells you exactly that, instead of a vague null. The classic case is an Android view that is only ready in `onCreate`.

Its limits, which get asked: it only works on a `var`, never on a `val`; it cannot be a nullable type (that would defeat the point); and it cannot be used on `Int`, `Double`, `Boolean` or the other primitive types, because those have no "empty" state to detect. To check whether it has been filled in, there is `this::prop.isInitialized`.

**`by lazy`** is a different idea: the value is worked out the **first time it is read**, and then kept. It goes with `val`, it is for something expensive you may not need at all, and by default it is safe to read from several threads at once — the first one works it out, the others wait.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
val s: String? = null
println(s?.length ?: -1)
questions.explanation: `?.` sees that `s` is null, so it does not call `length` and the whole thing becomes null. Then `?:` steps in and hands back the fallback, -1. The two together are the standard way of saying "the length, or this if there is nothing".
whyWrong: `null` is what you would get without the `?:`. It is there precisely so that nothing null comes out.
0 would be the length of empty text. There is no text at all here, which is a different thing — and that difference is often worth keeping.
Nothing crashes: `?.` is exactly the operator that stops the call from happening.

questions.prompt: What happens if you apply `!!` to a null value?
options: It gives back a default value
questions.explanation: `!!` means "I promise this is not null, and if I am wrong, stop". The promise being broken produces exactly the Java exception Kotlin was built to prevent — which is the point: it is you choosing to bring it back, so it should be rare and explainable.
whyWrong: `!!` never gives back null: its whole purpose is to produce a non-null value or stop.
There is no default value. Kotlin never invents one.
A different exception, used for other things. The one here is the null pointer, deliberately.

questions.prompt: Which `lateinit` declaration is valid?
questions.explanation: `lateinit` needs three things: a `var`, because it is assigned later; a non-nullable type, because being nullable would make it pointless; and a type that is not a primitive like `Int`, because those have no empty state the runtime could detect.
whyWrong: A `val` cannot be assigned later, which is the whole purpose of `lateinit`.
`Int` is not allowed: there is no "empty" value it could use to tell you it has not been set.
Pointless and refused: if the type can be null, use `?` and handle it. `lateinit` exists to avoid exactly that.

questions.prompt: How does `by lazy` behave with several threads, by default?
options: Synchronised: only one thread works it out, the others wait
Publication: several may work it out, the first result wins
questions.explanation: The default is the safe one: a lock makes sure the value is produced once, and anyone else arriving at the same moment waits for the result. The other modes exist for cases where you know the value is cheap or there is only one thread, and you want to avoid the lock.
whyWrong: That is `PUBLICATION`, which you have to ask for by name.
That is `NONE`, the fastest and the one with no protection. Also something you ask for.
It is safe by default, which is the opposite. The whole point is that you do not have to think about it.

questions.prompt: What happens when you compile this?
options: It does not compile: smart cast is impossible on a var property
questions.explanation: `item` is a `var` on another object, so something else could change it between the check and the use — another thread, or a method called in between. Kotlin refuses to assume. Copy it into a local `val` first, or use `b.item?.let { }`.
whyWrong: It never gets as far as printing: the program is not built.
It is an error, not a warning: Kotlin will not guess about something that might change underneath it.
It fails at compile time, which is the point — the crash is prevented before the program exists.

questions.prompt: A Java method `String getName()` has no annotations. What does Kotlin see?
questions.explanation: Java does not say whether the result can be null, so Kotlin does not know and does not check. That is the one hole in the guarantee: use it as non-null and nothing stops you, until one day it is null. The fix is to declare the type yourself on the Kotlin side.
whyWrong: Treating it as non-null would be a promise Kotlin has no basis for.
Treating it as nullable would be safe but would force a `?` on every Java call, which would be unbearable.
`Any?` would throw away the type as well as the nullability. Kotlin keeps the type; it is only the nullability it does not know.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
val name: String? = "Kotlin"
name?.let { println(it.uppercase()) }
questions.explanation: `?.let` runs the block only if there is something, and inside the block the value is called `it` and is non-null. There is text here, so the block runs and prints it upper-cased.
whyWrong: `uppercase()` changes it: lower case is what you started with.
`null` would mean `name` was empty. It is not.
Nothing would be printed only if `name` were null — that is exactly what `?.let` protects against.

questions.prompt: How do you check whether a `lateinit` property has been set?
questions.explanation: The property is not nullable, so comparing it with null is not even allowed. Kotlin gives you a check through a reference to the property itself: `this::prop.isInitialized`. It only works from inside the class that declares it.
whyWrong: It does not compile: the type is non-nullable, so that comparison makes no sense.
There is no such method on the value. The check lives on the property reference, not on the value.
Catching the exception would work but is clumsy, and there is a proper way.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The right-hand side of `?:` can be a `return`, which is what makes it so useful: either there is a value, or we leave immediately. `len(null)` returns 0, `len("ab")` returns 2, so the total is 2.
whyWrong: It compiles: a `return` on the right of `?:` is a normal Kotlin idiom.
The function returns `Int`, which can never be null.
0 is only what the first call gives. The second gives 2, and they are added.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
val x: String? = null
println(x + "!")
questions.explanation: Joining text calls `toString()`, and on a null reference Kotlin defines that as the four letters "null" rather than a crash. So you get `null!`. It is the reason a user occasionally sees the word "null" in an interface — nothing failed, it was just printed.
whyWrong: Nothing is skipped: the word "null" really does end up in the text.
This is exactly one of the cases where Kotlin does not crash, which is what makes it surprising.
It compiles: joining a nullable to text is allowed, precisely because the result is defined.

topics.title: Classes, data classes and sealed types
topics.summary: How to describe a thing in Kotlin: the class that only holds data, the one that lists the few shapes something can take, and the one there is only ever one of.

lesson.heading: Classes, and why they are closed by default
lesson.body:
A **class** describes a kind of thing: what it holds and what it can do. You create one with `class`, and the things it holds go in the brackets after the name — that is the **primary constructor**, and in Kotlin it declares the properties at the same time, in one line.

The decision that surprises people coming from Java: **a Kotlin class is `final` by default**. Nobody can inherit from it unless you write `open`. The same goes for methods.

It is deliberate, and the reasoning is worth knowing because it gets asked. A class that can be inherited from is a promise: you are saying that anyone may replace any part of it, and from then on you cannot change the inside without possibly breaking somebody. Most classes were never meant to carry that promise. Making it something you ask for means you only pay for it where you meant to.

The practical consequence: when you want to share behaviour, reach for an **interface** first. Kotlin interfaces can hold default implementations, so you get most of what a base class gave you, without the closed hierarchy — and a class can implement as many as it likes.

lesson.heading: Data classes: when the thing is its data
lesson.body:
Some classes exist only to hold values: a user, a message, a point. In Java that meant writing a constructor, getters, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` by hand — fifty lines where the information was two.

**`data class`** writes all of them for you. One line, and you get:

**`equals` and `hashCode`** based on the values, so two objects with the same contents count as the same thing. That is almost always what you want for data, and it is what lets them work properly in a `Set` or as a key in a map.

**`toString`** that actually shows the contents, which makes debugging bearable.

**`copy`** to make a changed version: `u.copy(name = "Bea")` gives you a new one with everything the same except the name. This is the basis of how state is handled in modern Android.

**Destructuring**, so you can write `val (id, name) = user`.

Two things worth knowing, because both get asked. Only the properties **in the constructor** take part in `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString` and `copy` — anything declared in the body is ignored, which surprises people. And `copy` is **shallow**: it copies the references, so a mutable list inside is shared between the original and the copy.
lesson.code:
data class User(val id: Int, val name: String)

val u = User(1, "Ann")
val v = u.copy(name = "Bea")     // a new one, name changed
val (id, name) = v               // destructuring
println(v)                       // User(id=1, name=Bea)
println(User(1, "Ann") == u)     // true: same contents

// Only what is in the constructor counts
data class Point(val x: Int) {
    var y: Int = 0               // ignored by equals, copy and toString
}

// copy is shallow: the list is shared
data class Team(val members: MutableList<String>)
val t1 = Team(mutableListOf("A"))
val t2 = t1.copy()
t2.members.add("B")
println(t1.members)              // [A, B] — the same list

lesson.heading: enum and sealed: listing the possibilities
lesson.body:
Often a value can only be one of a few known things: a state, a result, an error. Two tools for that, and choosing between them is a standard interview question.

**`enum class`** is a fixed list of constants. Each one is a single instance, they all carry the same kind of data, and you get `entries`, `ordinal` and `valueOf` for free. Right for a set of labels: days of the week, a status.

**`sealed`** is a list of **types**, which is much more powerful. Each case can be a different class carrying different data — and that is the point. "Loading" carries nothing, "Success" carries a list, "Error" carries a message. An enum cannot do that: every constant would have to have every field, most of them empty.

What they share, and the reason both exist: the compiler knows every case. So a `when` over them does not need an `else`, and — this is the real benefit — **the day somebody adds a case, every `when` that does not handle it stops compiling**. The compiler walks you to each place that needs updating, instead of you finding out from a user.

The rule of thumb: an enum when the cases are just names, a sealed type when they carry different data.

lesson.heading: object and companion object
lesson.body:
**`object`** declares a class and creates its one and only instance, in a single word. It is Kotlin's singleton, and it is safe to use from several threads without you doing anything — the language guarantees it is created once.

Use it for something there is genuinely only one of: a configuration, a registry, a small collection of helpers. Not as a convenient place to hang global state, which makes code hard to test for the usual reasons.

**`companion object`** is an object that lives inside a class. Since Kotlin has no `static`, this is where the things you reach through the class name go: constants, factory functions, the private constructor pattern.

And `object` has a third use, which is less obvious: **an anonymous object**, written `object : SomeInterface { }`, creates a one-off implementation on the spot. That is Kotlin's version of Java's anonymous inner class, and it is how you pass a listener that needs more than a single method.

lesson.heading: Value classes: a type that costs nothing
lesson.body:
A function that takes `(String, String, String)` is an invitation to pass them in the wrong order. Nothing stops you putting the email where the name goes, and the compiler is happy.

You could wrap each one in a class, and then the compiler would catch it — but you would be creating an object for every value, which for an id used everywhere is a real cost.

**A value class** gives you both. You write `@JvmInline value class UserId(val raw: String)`, and it is a proper type the compiler enforces — but when it compiles, the wrapper disappears and what is actually passed around is the plain `String`. The safety is free.

There is one thing to know, and it is the interview question: sometimes the wrapper has to come back. If the value goes somewhere that needs a real object — into a `List`, into a nullable, through a generic — it gets **boxed** and the cost returns. Used plainly as a parameter or a return value, it stays free.

The rule: wherever you have a `String` or an `Int` that means something specific — an id, a quantity, a currency — a value class makes it impossible to confuse with another one, at no cost.

questions.prompt: By default, a Kotlin class is:
questions.explanation: Visible to everyone, but closed to inheritance. Closed by default is deliberate: being inheritable is a promise about your internals, and you should make it on purpose, with `open`, rather than by accident.
whyWrong: Open by default is Java's choice. Kotlin reversed it precisely because most classes were never designed to be inherited from.
The default visibility is public, not internal. `internal` means "inside this module" and has to be asked for.
Wrong on both counts: it is closed, and it is visible to everyone.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: A data class only generates `equals` from the properties **in the constructor**. `age` is declared in the body, so it is ignored entirely: as far as `equals` is concerned, both are just "Ann", and they are equal. This catches people out regularly.
whyWrong: `false` is the intuitive answer, and it would be right if `age` were in the constructor. It is not.
It compiles: a data class is allowed to have properties in its body — they just do not take part.
`hashCode` is generated from the same properties as `equals`, so it agrees. There is nothing uncertain here.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
data class Team(val members: MutableList<String>)

val t1 = Team(mutableListOf("A"))
val t2 = t1.copy()
t2.members.add("B")
println(t1.members.size)
questions.explanation: `copy` is shallow: it copies the property, and the property is a reference to a list, not the list itself. So both teams point at the same list, and adding through one is visible through the other. If you want them separate, copy the list too: `copy(members = members.toMutableList())`.
whyWrong: 1 is what you would get if the copy went all the way down. It does not.
0 would mean the list was emptied, which nothing here does.
Nothing fails: adding to a shared list is perfectly legal. It is just not what you expected.

questions.prompt: How do you declare a singleton in Kotlin?
questions.explanation: `object` declares the class and creates its only instance at the same time. The language guarantees it is created once, safely, even with several threads — so none of the double-checked locking from Java is needed.
whyWrong: Kotlin has no `static` at all. Its job is done by `object` and `companion object`.
There is no such keyword.
A `companion object` lives inside another class. On its own it is not a declaration you can write.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of a sealed hierarchy in a `when`?
options: It can be extended from any module
It is faster than an enum
questions.explanation: The compiler knows every possible case, so it can check you handled them all. The real win comes later: when somebody adds a case, every `when` that does not handle it stops compiling, and the compiler walks you to each one.
whyWrong: Only the ones declared as `data object` are single instances. A `data class` case can have as many as you like.
It is the opposite: the cases have to be in the same module, and that is exactly what lets the compiler know them all.
Speed is not the point, and in practice there is nothing in it.

questions.prompt: Given `@JvmInline value class Meters(val v: Int)`, when does a `Meters` get boxed?
questions.explanation: A list holds objects, so the wrapper has to actually exist to go in one. In every other case here the compiler erases it and passes the plain `Int`. The same happens with a nullable `Meters?` and with generics, for the same reason.
whyWrong: As a parameter it is erased: what is really passed is the `Int`.
A local variable is erased too: there is no object.
As a return value it is erased as well.

questions.prompt: What is a `companion object` for?
options: It makes a second instance of the class
It defines an extension of the class
It holds members you reach through the class name
questions.explanation: Kotlin has no `static`, so the things that would have been static go here: constants, factory functions, anything you call as `MyClass.something()`. There is exactly one per class, and it is created with the class.
whyWrong: It creates no instance of the outer class. It is an object of its own, inside it.
Abstract is a separate keyword and a separate idea.
Extensions are written outside the class, with `fun MyClass.foo()`.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of a data class?
options: It must have at least two properties
It can extend an open class and implement interfaces
`equals` includes the properties in the body
questions.explanation: A data class can inherit and can implement interfaces — it is an ordinary class with some methods written for it. What it cannot be is `open`, because the generated `equals` assumes the exact type, and a subclass would break that promise.
whyWrong: It cannot: `open` and `data` do not go together, for exactly that reason.
One property is enough. Zero is not: there would be nothing to generate from.
Only the constructor properties count. Anything in the body is ignored, which is the trap in an earlier question.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer a sealed type over an enum?
options: When the cases carry different data, or there can be more than one of a case
questions.explanation: That is the dividing line. An enum has one instance per constant and the same shape for all of them. A sealed type lets "Success" carry a list and "Error" carry a message — and lets you create as many `Error`s as you like, each with its own text.
whyWrong: For plain constants an enum is simpler and gives you more for free.
`ordinal` is an enum feature. Needing it is a reason to use an enum.
`entries` is also an enum feature, for listing the values.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
options: It does not compile: interfaces cannot have properties
questions.explanation: A Kotlin interface can declare properties and can give them a default implementation, as long as it is computed rather than stored. `greeting` is worked out each time it is read, using whatever `name` the class provided — here "Bo".
whyWrong: `name` is not null: the class provides it with `override val name = "Bo"`.
They can: what an interface cannot do is **store** a value. A computed property like this is fine.
It is not empty: the class supplied a name.

topics.title: Lambdas, extensions and scope functions
topics.summary: Passing a block of code as a value, adding a method to a type you do not own, and the five little functions every Kotlin file is full of.

lesson.heading: A function can be a value
lesson.body:
In Kotlin a function is a value like any other: you can put it in a variable, pass it to another function, hand it back from one. A function that takes or returns a function is a **higher-order function**.

A function type is written with an arrow: `(Int) -> Int` is "takes a number, gives back a number". `() -> Unit` is "takes nothing, gives back nothing" — the type of a callback.

A **lambda** is a function with no name, written in braces: `{ x -> x * 2 }`. Two shortcuts make them short enough to read at a glance. If there is exactly one parameter, you can leave the name out and call it **`it`**. And if the lambda is the **last** argument, it can go outside the brackets — which is what makes `list.filter { it > 2 }` look the way it does, with no brackets in sight.

There is also `::name`, a **reference** to a function that already exists, for when you would otherwise write a lambda that does nothing but call it.

lesson.heading: inline: lambdas that cost nothing
lesson.body:
On the JVM, a lambda is normally an object. Pass one in a loop that runs ten thousand times and you have created ten thousand objects for a block of code that never changes.

**`inline`** removes that. The compiler takes the body of the function and the body of the lambda and **copies them into the call site**. No object, no call, no cost. That is why `map`, `filter` and `forEach` are free compared with a hand-written loop.

It buys you a second thing, which is the part people notice first. Because the lambda's body ends up literally inside your function, a `return` inside it returns from **your function**, not just from the lambda. That is a **non-local return**, and it is why `forEach` with a `return` inside behaves like a real loop with a `break`.

When not to use it: a long function, because its body is copied to every call site and the code grows. It is for short functions that take lambdas, which is exactly what the standard library uses it for.

And two modifiers you will meet: **`noinline`** on a parameter that must stay a real object — because you want to store it — and **`crossinline`** on one that is called from somewhere else, which forbids the non-local return because there would be nothing to return from.

lesson.heading: reified: knowing the type at runtime
lesson.body:
On the JVM, generic types are **erased**: at runtime a `List<String>` is just a `List`, and the `String` is gone. So inside a generic function you cannot ask "is this a T?", because nothing knows what T was.

The traditional workaround is to pass the class as an extra argument — `Gson().fromJson(json, User::class.java)` — which is clumsy and easy to get wrong.

**`reified`** fixes it, and the way it works follows directly from `inline`. Because the function's body is copied into the call site, and at the call site the compiler **does** know the real type, it can substitute it there. So the type survives, and `is T` works.

That is why `reified` can only be used on an `inline` function: there is nowhere to substitute the type otherwise. It is one of the most satisfying questions to be able to answer, because the reason is so direct.
lesson.code:
inline fun <reified T> List<*>.firstOfType(): T? =
    firstOrNull { it is T } as T?      // 'is T' works thanks to reified

val s = listOf(1, "a", 2.0).firstOfType<String>()   // "a"

// Without reified, the type has to be passed by hand
fun <T> parse(json: String, type: Class<T>): T = gson.fromJson(json, type)
parse(json, User::class.java)

// With reified, the call reads properly
inline fun <reified T> parse(json: String): T = gson.fromJson(json, T::class.java)
val user: User = parse(json)

lesson.heading: Extension functions
lesson.body:
An **extension function** adds a method to a type you do not own. You write `fun String.initials()` and from then on every string has an `initials()`, including ones from libraries you cannot change.

Inside it, `this` is the object it was called on, and you can leave `this` out.

The important thing — and the interview question — is that **nothing is really added to the type**. The compiler turns it into an ordinary function that takes the object as its first argument. From that, two consequences follow, and both get asked:

**They are resolved by the declared type, not the real one.** If you have an extension on `A` and one on `B`, and a variable declared as `A` holding a `B`, you get `A`'s. There is no overriding, because there is nothing to override. Real methods behave the opposite way.

**A real method always wins.** If the class already has a method with that name, yours is never called — and the compiler only gives you a warning, so it is easy to miss.

Used well, they are what keeps Kotlin code readable: small, well-named operations that belong to a type conceptually without having to live inside it.
lesson.code:
fun String.initials(): String =
    split(" ").mapNotNull { it.firstOrNull() }.joinToString("")

println("Ada Lovelace".initials())    // AL

// Resolved by the declared type, not the real one
open class A
class B : A()
fun A.name() = "A"
fun B.name() = "B"

val x: A = B()
println(x.name())        // "A" — decided at compile time

// A real method always wins over an extension
class C { fun hi() = "member" }
fun C.hi() = "extension"
println(C().hi())        // "member"

lesson.heading: The five scope functions
lesson.body:
`let`, `run`, `with`, `apply`, `also`. They all do the same shape of thing — run a block on an object — and they differ in two ways only. Learn the two and you will never have to memorise the five.

**How you refer to the object:** as `it` (a normal parameter) or as `this` (you can leave it out entirely).

**What you get back:** the object itself, or the result of the block.

From that:

**`let`** — `it`, gives back the block's result. The everyday use is `?.let { }`: do this only if there is something.
**`run`** — `this`, gives back the block's result. For working out a value using several of the object's properties.
**`apply`** — `this`, gives back the object. For configuring something and keeping it: it is the one you want when building an object with several properties to set.
**`also`** — `it`, gives back the object. For doing something on the side — logging, validating — without changing what is being passed along.
**`with`** — like `run`, but written as `with(obj) { }` rather than `obj.run { }`.

The practical shortcut: **`apply` to configure, `also` to look, `let` for null, `run` to calculate.**

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `let` hands back what the block produced, which is the length, 6. `also` hands back the object it was called on, whatever the block did — so `s` is still the text. That is the only difference between the two.
whyWrong: They cannot both give 6: `also` always gives back the object.
They cannot both give the text: `let` always gives back the block's result.
They are the wrong way round: `let` gives the result, `also` gives the object.

questions.prompt: Which scope function uses `this` and gives back the object itself?
questions.explanation: `apply` is the configuring one: inside the block the object is `this` so you can leave it out, and at the end you get the object back, ready to assign. It is what you use to build something with several properties to set.
whyWrong: `let` uses `it` and gives back the block's result.
`run` uses `this` but gives back the block's result, not the object.
`also` gives back the object but uses `it`, not `this`.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
open class A
class B : A()

fun A.name() = "A"
fun B.name() = "B"

val x: A = B()
println(x.name())
questions.explanation: Extensions are not really added to the type: the compiler turns them into ordinary functions and picks one from the **declared** type. `x` is declared as `A`, so `A`'s extension is chosen, even though the object is a `B`. A real method would have behaved the other way round.
whyWrong: `B` would be right for a real method, where the real type decides at runtime. Extensions are decided while compiling.
Only one is called, not both.
It compiles: two extensions with the same name on different types is perfectly normal.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: A real method always wins. The extension is simply never called — and the compiler only warns you, which is why this is easy to miss when somebody adds a method to a class you had extended.
whyWrong: The extension would only be used if the class had no such method.
There is no ambiguity: the rule is clear and the member wins.
Only one is called. Nothing is joined together.

questions.prompt: Why does `reified` require an `inline` function?
options: The real type is substituted at the call site, which only inlining makes possible
Non-inline functions do not support generics
questions.explanation: Generic types are erased on the JVM, so at runtime nothing knows what T was. Inlining copies the function body into the call site, and there the compiler does know the real type, so it can put it in. Without inlining there is nowhere to do the substitution.
whyWrong: No reflection is involved: it all happens while compiling, which is why it costs nothing.
Generics work in any function. What does not survive to runtime is the type argument.
Boxing is a separate matter and has nothing to do with it.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `forEach` is `inline`, so the lambda's body ends up literally inside `find`. That means the `return` is a return from `find` itself — a non-local return — and the last line is never reached. It behaves exactly like a real loop with a `break`.
whyWrong: `none` would require the `return` to leave only the lambda, which is what `return@forEach` does.
It compiles: the non-local return is a deliberate feature of inline functions.
A function returns once. It cannot print both.

questions.prompt: What does `crossinline` do on a lambda parameter?
options: Lets you store it in a field
questions.explanation: It is for a lambda that is inlined but called from somewhere else — inside another lambda, or in a `Runnable`. A `return` from the outer function would make no sense there, because that function may already have finished. `crossinline` forbids it while keeping the inlining.
whyWrong: That is `noinline`, which turns it back into a real object.
Threads have nothing to do with it.
Storing it needs `noinline`, because you need a real object to store.

questions.prompt: In a lambda with one parameter, what is `it`?
options: The implicit name of that single parameter
The receiver of the outer function
questions.explanation: When there is exactly one parameter you can leave the name out, and Kotlin calls it `it`. It keeps short lambdas short. With two or more parameters you have to name them.
whyWrong: The receiver is `this`, and only in the scope functions that provide one.
The result is what the last expression produces: it has no name.
There is no iterator in sight: `it` is the current element, not the thing walking over them.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `return@forEach` leaves only the current pass of the lambda, like a `continue` in a loop. So 2 is skipped and 1 and 3 are printed. Without the label, the `return` would have left the whole enclosing function.
whyWrong: 1 alone would mean it stopped at 2, which is what a bare `return` would do.
123 would mean nothing was skipped, and 2 is explicitly skipped.
12 would mean it stopped after 2, which is neither of the two behaviours.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of `inline` on a function that takes a lambda?
options: It always makes the compiled code smaller
It avoids creating an object for the lambda
questions.explanation: Without inlining, every lambda becomes an object on the JVM. Inside a loop that is thousands of objects for a block of code that never changes. Inlining copies the code in instead, so nothing is created — which is why `map` and `filter` cost the same as a hand-written loop.
whyWrong: It usually makes it bigger, because the body is copied to every call site. That is the cost you accept.
Recursion is unrelated, and an inline function cannot sensibly be recursive.
`open` is about inheritance and has nothing to do with this.

topics.title: Collections and sequences
topics.summary: Lists, sets and maps, the handful of operators you use every day, and the one word that stops a chain over a million items from building a million-item list each step.

lesson.heading: Read-only is not the same as unchangeable
lesson.body:
Kotlin has two names for a list. **`List`** has no methods for adding or removing. **`MutableList`** has them.

That is the first thing to get right, because the names mislead: a `List` is a **read-only view**, not a promise that nothing will ever change. If somebody else is holding the same object as a `MutableList`, they can change it, and your "read-only" list changes underneath you.

So `List` means "**I** cannot change this", not "this cannot change".

If you want a genuine guarantee, make a copy — `toList()` — and hold that. Then nobody has a reference to the same object.

The practical rules worth adopting: **always declare `List` unless you really need to add things**. Return `List` from functions and properties, never `MutableList`, so a caller cannot change your internals. And if the contents must not change, copy on the way out.

And a warning: because `List` and `MutableList` are the same object underneath, you can cast one to the other. It compiles, it sometimes even works, and it is a sure way to produce a bug nobody can find.

lesson.heading: The operators you will use every day
lesson.body:
Instead of writing a loop and growing a result by hand, you say what you want. The code gets shorter, and the name tells the reader what is going on.

**`map`** — one result per element, same length.
**`filter`** — keep the ones that pass a test.
**`first { }` / `find { }`** — the first match; `first` throws if there is none, `find` gives `null`.
**`any` / `all` / `none`** — a yes-or-no about the whole collection.
**`sumOf` / `maxByOrNull` / `sortedBy`** — the usual summaries and orderings.

Three that are worth knowing properly because they are confused with each other:

**`groupBy`** gives a map from key to **list** — "all the words starting with a".
**`associateBy`** gives a map from key to **one element** — and when two elements share a key, **the last one silently wins**. That is the trap.
**`associateWith`** goes the other way: the elements are the keys, and you work out the values.

And **`fold`** versus **`reduce`**: `fold` takes a starting value, `reduce` uses the first element as the start. So `reduce` on an empty collection has nothing to start from and throws. `fold` on an empty collection calmly gives you the starting value. Prefer `fold`.

lesson.heading: Sequence: do the work only when it is needed
lesson.body:
A chain on a `List` builds a new list at every step. `map` then `filter` over a million items means two million-item lists created and thrown away, and all two million maps run even if you only wanted the first result.

**`asSequence()`** changes how the work is organised. A sequence builds nothing: it passes **one element at a time** all the way down the chain, then the next. Combine that with something that stops early — `first`, `take`, `find` — and almost all the work simply never happens.

The order of the output is the giveaway, and it is the classic question. On a list you see all the maps, then all the filters. On a sequence you see map, filter, map, filter — one element going the whole way before the next starts.

When it is worth it: many elements, several steps chained, or an early stop. When it is not: a short list, where the extra bookkeeping costs more than it saves — and in that case a list is faster.

One last thing: a sequence is **lazy**, so nothing happens at all until you ask for a result. The operation that asks is called terminal — `toList`, `first`, `sum`, `forEach`. Without one, you have described some work and never run it.

lesson.heading: Choosing the right collection
lesson.body:
Three kinds, and picking the wrong one is the usual cause of code that is slow for no reason.

**`List`** — things in order, duplicates allowed, instant access by position. Scanning it to find something takes as long as the list is.

**`Set`** — unique things, no order, and **instant** "is this in here?". That one property is the whole reason it exists.

**`Map`** — key to value, instant lookup by key.

The mistake worth learning to spot: `contains` inside a loop over a list. If both lists have a thousand items, that is a million comparisons. Turning the inner one into a `Set` first makes it a thousand. It is one line, and it is the most common performance fix at this level.

Two other things worth knowing. `LinkedHashMap` — which is what `mapOf` actually gives you — keeps the order things were put in, so iterating a Kotlin map is predictable, unlike in some other languages. And `buildList { }` lets you build a list with a mutable one inside and hand back a read-only one, without the usual two-variable dance.

lesson.heading: The traps that come up at interview
lesson.body:
Five things that are asked over and over, collected in one place.

**`associateBy` loses duplicates.** Two elements with the same key, and the last one wins, silently. If that matters, use `groupBy`.

**`reduce` throws on an empty collection.** It uses the first element as the starting value, and there is not one. `fold` takes a starting value and is safe.

**`List` is not immutable.** It is a read-only view of something that might be mutable elsewhere.

**A `Sequence` can only be walked once** if it came from an iterator — `asSequence()` on a list is fine, but one built from a stream is consumed. Walking it twice gives you an exception or nothing at all.

**`sortedBy` makes a new list; `sortBy` changes the one you have.** The same pattern runs right through: `sorted`, `reversed`, `shuffled` give you a copy, while `sort`, `reverse`, `shuffle` change the original in place and only exist on a `MutableList`. Mixing them up means your sort appears to do nothing, because you threw away the result.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code: println(listOf(1, 2, 3).map { it * 2 }.filter { it > 2 })
questions.explanation: `map` doubles everything first, giving `[2, 4, 6]`. Then `filter` keeps only what is above 2, which drops the 2 and leaves `[4, 6]`. The order matters: filtering first would have given a different answer.
whyWrong: That is the result after `map`, before the filter ran.
[6] would be what is above 4. The test is above 2.
[3] is not produced by any step here.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
options: m1 m2 m3 f1 f2 f3
m1 f1 m2 f2 m3 f3
questions.explanation: A sequence sends one element all the way down the chain before starting the next. The 1 is mapped, filtered and rejected; the 2 is mapped, filtered and accepted — and `first` has what it wants, so it stops. The 3 is never touched.
whyWrong: That is what a list does: every map, then every filter.
`first` is a terminal operation, so the work does run. Nothing would happen only without one.
The 3 is never reached: `first` stopped as soon as it had a match.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
val r = listOf(1, 2, 3).fold(10) { acc, x -> acc + x }
println(r)
questions.explanation: `fold` starts from the value you give it, 10, and adds each element: 10 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 16. That starting value is the whole difference from `reduce`, which would start from the first element and give 6.
whyWrong: 6 is what `reduce` gives, starting from the first element rather than from 10.
10 would mean nothing was added. The whole list takes part.
It compiles: this is exactly what `fold` is for.

questions.prompt: What does the type `List<T>` guarantee?
options: A read-only view: no guarantee that it cannot change
That it is a fixed-size array
That it is safe to use from several threads
questions.explanation: `List` only means you have no methods for changing it. The object underneath may well be a `MutableList` that somebody else is holding and changing. For a real guarantee, make a copy with `toList()`.
whyWrong: Nothing about `List` promises that. Kotlin has no deeply immutable collection in the standard library.
It is not an array and its size can change — through whoever holds it as mutable.
Thread safety is a separate question, and a `List` gives you none.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `groupBy` makes a map from key to **list**, so nothing is lost: under 'a' there are both apple and avocado, which is 2. `associateBy` would have given a single element and silently dropped one.
whyWrong: 1 is what `associateBy` would leave, since it keeps only the last.
3 is the total number of words. They are split across two keys.
The key is there, so it is not null.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
val list: List<Int> = mutableListOf(1, 2)
(list as MutableList<Int>).add(3)
println(list)
questions.explanation: The object really is a `MutableList`: `List` was only how it was being seen. The cast succeeds and the add works. It compiles and it runs — and it is exactly the kind of thing that produces a bug nobody can trace, which is why you should never do it.
whyWrong: The add really happens: the list afterwards has three elements.
Nothing fails: the object is genuinely of that type.
That would happen on a list from `listOf`, which really is unchangeable. This one came from `mutableListOf`.

questions.prompt: What does `listOf("a", "ab", "b").associateBy { it.first() }` give?
questions.explanation: `associateBy` maps each key to a single element, so when two share a key the last one wins — silently. "a" and "ab" both have key 'a', and "ab" comes later, so "a" disappears. If you need both, use `groupBy`.
whyWrong: Lists as values is what `groupBy` gives. `associateBy` keeps one element per key.
No exception: it quietly overwrites, which is what makes it dangerous.
"a" is the one that is lost, not the one that is kept: later wins.

questions.prompt: When is a `Sequence` better than a `List`?
options: Short lists with a single operation
When you need access by position
Several operations chained over many elements, or when you stop early
Always: it is faster in every case
questions.explanation: A sequence pays off when it can avoid work: no intermediate lists, and nothing computed past the point where you stopped. On a short list the extra bookkeeping costs more than it saves, and a plain list wins.
whyWrong: With one operation on a short list, a list is faster.
A sequence has no access by position at all: you can only walk through it.
"Always" is wrong, and it is the trap: on small collections a list is the faster choice.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
val (even, odd) = (1..5).partition { it % 2 == 0 }
println(odd)
questions.explanation: `partition` gives back a pair: first those that pass the test, then those that do not. The test is "even", so the first part is the even ones and the second — which is `odd` here — is the odd ones.
whyWrong: [2, 4] is the first part, which went into `even`.
3 would be a count, and `partition` hands back lists.
It hands back a pair of lists, and destructuring has already split it into two names.

questions.prompt: What happens here?
questions.code: println(emptyList<Int>().reduce { a, b -> a + b })
questions.explanation: `reduce` uses the first element as its starting value, and there is no first element. It has nothing to return and no sensible default to invent, so it throws. `fold(0)` would have given you 0 calmly, which is why it is the safer choice.
whyWrong: 0 would require a starting value, and `reduce` does not take one. That is `fold`.
The function returns `Int`, which cannot be null.
That is the exception for an operation that is not supported. Here the operation is fine; the collection is empty.

topics.title: The life of an Android screen
topics.summary: Why rotating the phone destroys your screen and rebuilds it, what survives that and what does not, and where the state actually has to live.

lesson.heading: The Activity lifecycle
lesson.body:
An **Activity** is one screen of an Android app. The system creates it, shows it, hides it and destroys it — and tells you at every step, so you can prepare and tidy up.

The sequence when a screen opens:

**`onCreate`** — it exists. Runs **once**. Build the interface, connect the ViewModel.
**`onStart`** — it is about to be visible.
**`onResume`** — it is in front and receiving taps.

And on the way out, in reverse: `onPause` (something is covering it), `onStop` (no longer visible), `onDestroy` (gone).

The thing to hold on to is the pairing: **what you start in one, you stop in the matching one**. Start a camera in `onResume`, release it in `onPause`. Register a listener in `onStart`, remove it in `onStop`. Things that live as long as the screen go in `onCreate` and `onDestroy`.

And the timing detail people get wrong: when screen A opens screen B, **A does not stop until B is on screen**. The order is A.onPause, B.onCreate, B.onStart, B.onResume, then A.onStop. So `onPause` is short and must stay fast, while `onStop` is where the real tidying goes.

lesson.heading: Rotation destroys everything
lesson.body:
Turn the phone sideways and Android **destroys the Activity and builds a new one**. Not a resize: a different object, from `onCreate` again.

It looks absurd until you see why. A different orientation may need a different layout, different images, different text lengths. Rather than ask every app to handle that, the system throws the screen away and rebuilds it with the right resources. The same thing happens when the language changes, when dark mode is switched on, when the window is resized on a foldable.

The consequence is the one that bites: **anything you were holding in a field of the Activity is gone**. The list you had downloaded, what the user had typed, the scroll position. Rotate the phone and the app starts over.

There are three ways to survive it, and they are not alternatives — they answer different questions:

**ViewModel** — survives rotation. It is where the data and the state of the screen go.
**`onSaveInstanceState`** and **`SavedStateHandle`** — survive rotation **and** the process being killed, because they are actually written to disk. Small things only.
**Nothing** — if it can be worked out again cheaply.

And a warning: `android:configChanges` in the manifest stops the rebuild, which makes the problem look solved. It is not. It only hides it, and it stops the system giving you the right resources.

lesson.heading: Process death: the case nobody tests
lesson.body:
The user leaves your app, opens three others, comes back twenty minutes later. In between, Android needed memory and **killed your process**.

When they come back, the system does not start from the home screen: it recreates the screen they were on, to make it feel as if the app never went away. But everything in memory is gone, **including the ViewModel** — that is the crucial point, because a ViewModel survives rotation but not this.

What does survive is only what was written down: `onSaveInstanceState`, `SavedStateHandle`, and anything you actually put in a database or in preferences.

The reason this matters more than it seems is that it never happens to you while you are developing. The phone has memory, the app stays alive, and the bug ships. Then it happens to users on older phones, and the report says "it loses my data sometimes", which is impossible to reproduce.

To test it on purpose: put the app in the background and run `adb shell am kill <package>`. Then reopen it from the task switcher — not from the icon, because that would start fresh. If the screen comes back empty, you have found it.

The rule for what to save: **small and essential**. An id, a search query, which tab was open. Never a bitmap or a long list — there is a size limit, and going over it crashes the app.

lesson.heading: Fragments: two lifecycles, not one
lesson.body:
A **Fragment** is a reusable piece of a screen. It has its own lifecycle, and the detail that causes most of the leaks in Android is that it really has **two**.

**The Fragment's own lifecycle** — from `onCreate` to `onDestroy`.
**Its view's lifecycle** — from `onCreateView` to `onDestroyView`.

They are not the same, and the gap between them is where the trouble is. When a fragment is put on the back stack, **its view is destroyed but the fragment itself stays alive**. Later, when the user comes back, a new view is created for the same fragment.

So if you observed something using the fragment as the owner, that observation survives the view and keeps running — pointing at views that no longer exist. Come back and forth a few times and you have several observers all updating dead views.

The two rules that follow, and they are the ones to remember:

**Observe with `viewLifecycleOwner`, never with `this`.** The observation then ends when the view does.

**Clear the binding in `onDestroyView`.** A `ViewBinding` holds every view in the layout; keeping it means keeping the whole layout in memory for as long as the fragment lives.

lesson.heading: Intents: opening something else
lesson.body:
An **Intent** is how you ask for something to happen: open another screen, share a link, take a photo.

**Explicit** — you name exactly which class to open. For moving around inside your own app.
**Implicit** — you describe what you want and let the system find whoever can do it. For sharing, opening a link, picking a photo. Android shows the user the choice.

For results from another app, the old `startActivityForResult` is gone. The replacement is the **Activity Result API**: you register a contract in advance and get a launcher. It has to be registered while the screen is being created, not at the moment of the tap, because after process death the registration must happen again before the result arrives.

And one thing that broke a lot of apps on Android 12: a **`PendingIntent`** — an intent you hand to the system to run later, for a notification or an alarm — now **must** say `FLAG_IMMUTABLE` or `FLAG_MUTABLE`. Without one of them the app crashes on creation. Use `IMMUTABLE` unless something genuinely has to fill in the intent for you.

questions.prompt: In what order are the callbacks called when an Activity starts?
questions.explanation: It follows the stages: it exists (`onCreate`), it is about to be visible (`onStart`), it is in front and receiving taps (`onResume`). Only `onCreate` runs once; the other two run again every time the screen comes back.
whyWrong: `onResume` cannot come before `onStart`: you have to be visible before you can be in front.
`onCreate` is always first: nothing else can happen before the screen exists.
That is the whole thing backwards.

questions.prompt: What happens to an Activity when you rotate the screen, by default?
options: Nothing, the layout is just recalculated
It is destroyed and a new one is created
questions.explanation: Android destroys the Activity and builds a new one from `onCreate`, so it can load the resources for the new orientation — a different layout, different images. That is why anything held in a field of the Activity is lost, and why ViewModels exist.
whyWrong: It would be simpler, but then an app could not have a different layout for landscape.
The process stays alive: only the Activity is rebuilt. Killing the process is a different event.
The whole sequence runs, right through to `onDestroy`, and then a new object starts from `onCreate`.

questions.prompt: What does a ViewModel survive?
options: Both rotation and the process being killed
Rotation, but not the process being killed
questions.explanation: A ViewModel lives in memory, attached to the screen rather than to the Activity object, so it comes through a rebuild. But when the system kills the process, memory goes with it. For that you need `SavedStateHandle`, which is actually written to disk.
whyWrong: Surviving a killed process would need the data to be written down. A ViewModel only lives in memory.
It is the other way round: rotation is exactly what it does survive.
It survives rotation, which is the problem it was built to solve.

questions.prompt: Why do you observe with `viewLifecycleOwner` in a Fragment, and not with `this`?
options: The view can be destroyed while the fragment stays alive
Because `this` is not a lifecycle owner
It is only needed with Compose
questions.explanation: A fragment on the back stack keeps living while its view is destroyed. An observation tied to the fragment survives the view and goes on updating views that no longer exist — and a new one is added each time you come back. `viewLifecycleOwner` ends with the view, as it should.
whyWrong: The fragment is a lifecycle owner: that is exactly why it compiles, and why the bug is quiet.
Speed has nothing to do with it. It is about when the observation stops.
It applies to Fragments in general. With Compose the problem does not arise in the same way.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a `SavedStateHandle`?
options: Small pieces of state: an id, a search query
questions.explanation: It is written to disk by the system, and there is a size limit — going over it crashes the app. So: ids, a query, which tab was open. The real data gets fetched again from the database or the network using what you saved.
whyWrong: Far too big, and over the limit it crashes. Keep the id and fetch the image again.
Keeping a Context is a leak, and it could not be written to disk anyway.
A connection cannot be saved and restored: it has to be opened again.

questions.prompt: Activity A opens a full-screen B. When is `A.onStop` called?
questions.explanation: Android does not hide A until B is actually on screen, so there is no empty moment in between. The order is A.onPause, B.onCreate, B.onStart, B.onResume, then A.onStop. That is why `onPause` must be quick — it is holding up the next screen — and why real tidying goes in `onStop`.
whyWrong: That would leave the screen blank while B is being built.
In between, the whole of B's startup happens.
A does reach `onStop`: it is no longer visible once B covers it.

questions.prompt: How do you reliably reproduce process death?
options: App in the background, then `adb shell am kill <package>`
questions.explanation: It has to be the process that is killed, not the screen — and then you reopen from the task switcher, so the system restores the screen the user was on. If it comes back empty, you have found the bug that never shows up on your own phone.
whyWrong: Rotation rebuilds the Activity but keeps the process, so the ViewModel survives: a different case.
Back closes the screen on purpose, which is not the same as being killed.
`finish()` is also a deliberate close, with no restore afterwards.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an implicit Intent?
questions.explanation: It names an action and some data rather than a class, so the system finds whoever can handle it — a browser, in this case. If there are several, the user picks. The other three all name exactly what to open, which makes them explicit.
whyWrong: Naming the class is the definition of explicit.
`setClass` does the same thing as the first, written differently.
`setComponent` is even more specific: it names the exact component.

questions.prompt: What is compulsory when creating a `PendingIntent` from Android 12 onwards?
questions.explanation: A `PendingIntent` is run later by somebody else, so leaving it changeable was a security hole: another app could fill in the gaps. Android 12 made the choice compulsory, and the app crashes on creation if neither flag is given. Use `IMMUTABLE` unless you genuinely need the other.
whyWrong: `UPDATE_CURRENT` is about reusing an existing one, and it does not satisfy the new requirement.
No permission is involved.
They are still there and still used, for notifications and alarms. What changed is this requirement.

questions.prompt: Where do you clear a Fragment's binding to avoid a leak?
questions.explanation: The binding holds every view in the layout, and the view dies in `onDestroyView` while the fragment carries on. Not clearing it there means the whole layout stays in memory for as long as the fragment lives — which, on the back stack, can be a long time.
whyWrong: `onDestroy` is for the fragment, and comes much later. By then the views have been dead for ages.
`onDetach` is later still, when the fragment leaves the Activity.
`onStop` means no longer visible, but the view still exists and may be shown again.

topics.title: Coroutines: waiting without blocking
topics.summary: How to do something slow without freezing the screen, who waits for whom, and why cancelling does not always stop anything.

lesson.heading: suspend: a function that can pause
lesson.body:
Downloading, reading a database, waiting a second: all of these take time. Do them on the **main thread** — the one that draws the interface — and the app freezes.

The old answer was a thread, or a callback. A thread is expensive: each one costs about a megabyte, and a phone cannot have thousands. Callbacks work but nest, and after three steps the code is unreadable.

A **coroutine** is a piece of work that can **pause and start again later**, and while it is paused the thread it was on is free to do something else. Thousands of coroutines can share a handful of threads, because most of them are waiting rather than working.

**`suspend`** marks a function that can pause. It can only be called from inside a coroutine or from another `suspend` function — the compiler enforces that chain, so it is impossible to call one by accident from somewhere that cannot handle the pause.

The key thing to understand: **`suspend` does not mean "on another thread"**. It means "can pause". Choosing a thread is a separate decision, and it is made with `withContext`.

lesson.heading: launch and async
lesson.body:
Two ways to start a coroutine, and the difference is simply whether there is a result.

**`launch`** — start something and do not wait for an answer. It gives back a **`Job`**, which is a handle you can use to cancel it or wait for it to finish. For anything whose result you do not need: saving, logging, reacting to a tap.

**`async`** — start something that produces a value. It gives back a **`Deferred`**, which is a promise of that value, and you call `await()` to collect it.

The real use of `async` is doing two things at once. Two `suspend` calls one after the other happen in sequence: two seconds for two one-second calls. Start them both with `async` and only `await` afterwards, and the two overlap: one second in total.

The mistake to avoid is `async` followed immediately by `await` on the next line. That starts something and waits for it at once, which is exactly what a plain call does, with extra machinery. `async` only pays off when there are at least two of them before the first `await`.

lesson.heading: Dispatchers: which thread the work runs on
lesson.body:
A **dispatcher** decides which thread a coroutine actually runs on. There are three you use, and choosing between them is a standard question.

**`Dispatchers.Main`** — the interface thread. Everything that touches the screen. On Android, `viewModelScope` and `lifecycleScope` already start here, which is why you can update the state without doing anything special.

**`Dispatchers.IO`** — for waiting on something outside: the network, the disk, a database. The pool is large, because these threads spend their time waiting rather than working, so having many costs little.

**`Dispatchers.Default`** — for work that actually uses the processor: sorting a large list, parsing, image work. The pool is about the size of the number of cores, because more threads than cores does not make calculation faster.

The rule, which also answers "where do I put `withContext`?": **the function decides for itself**. A repository function that reads the database puts `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` inside itself, so whoever calls it does not have to know or care. That is called being main-safe, and it means a caller can call it from anywhere without thinking.

lesson.heading: Structured concurrency: nothing gets lost
lesson.body:
The idea that makes coroutines safer than threads is that **every coroutine has a parent**, and from that three guarantees follow.

**A parent does not finish until its children have.** No work carries on after the thing that started it has gone.
**Cancelling a parent cancels its children.** When a screen closes, everything it started stops. You do not have to remember.
**A child's failure reaches the parent.** Nothing fails in silence.

A **scope** is what provides the parent. On Android you are given two: **`viewModelScope`**, cancelled when the ViewModel goes, and **`lifecycleScope`**, cancelled with the screen. Use them and cancellation is handled for you.

And the one to avoid: **`GlobalScope`**. It has no parent, so nothing cancels it, and its work can outlive the screen, the user leaving, everything. It is a leak with a convenient name.

The difference between **`coroutineScope`** and **`supervisorScope`** comes from the same idea. In a plain scope, one child failing cancels its siblings — right when you need all the results. In a supervisor scope the siblings carry on — right when the parts are independent, like loading three sections of a page where one failing should not blank the other two.

lesson.heading: Cancellation is cooperative
lesson.body:
