`job.cancel()` does not stop anything. It raises a flag, and the coroutine has to notice.

Everything in the coroutines library checks it: `delay`, `withContext`, anything `suspend` from the standard library. So in normal code cancellation works and you never think about it.

But a loop doing calculation calls none of those. It just carries on, happily, after the screen has closed. The fix is to check: `ensureActive()` throws if it has been cancelled, `isActive` just asks.

The second half, and the bug that catches everybody: **cancellation travels as an exception**, `CancellationException`. So a `catch (e: Exception)` around your work catches the cancellation too, swallows it, and the coroutine carries on running as if nothing had happened — which is exactly what you were trying to stop.

There are two ways out: catch only the specific exceptions you expect, or catch `CancellationException` first and rethrow it. The first is better, and the habit worth building is to never write a bare `catch (e: Exception)` inside a coroutine.

questions.prompt: What do `launch` and `async` give back?
options: launch a Deferred, async a Job
launch a Job, async a Deferred
questions.explanation: `launch` is for work with no result, so it gives back a `Job`: a handle for cancelling or waiting. `async` produces a value, so it gives back a `Deferred`, which is a `Job` that also carries a result you collect with `await()`.
whyWrong: They are the wrong way round: the one that carries a value is `async`.
A plain `Job` has no result, so `async` could not hand its value back.
A `Deferred` from `launch` would mean there was a value, and there is not.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `launch` starts the coroutine and carries straight on, so B is printed first. Then the outer code waits 200 ms, during which the inner one's 100 ms elapses and A is printed. At 200 ms, C. So B, A, C.
whyWrong: A first would mean `launch` blocked until it was done, which is precisely what it does not do.
C cannot come before A: it waits 200 ms, and A only needs 100.
A cannot come first, for the same reason as the first option.

questions.prompt: Which dispatcher for a database query or a network call?
questions.explanation: `IO` is for waiting on something outside the app: network, disk, database. Its pool is large on purpose, because these threads spend their time waiting rather than working, so having many of them costs little.
whyWrong: `Main` is the interface thread. Putting a slow call there is exactly what freezes the app.
`Default` is for work that uses the processor: sorting, parsing. Its pool is small, about the number of cores.
`Unconfined` is a special case for libraries and tests. It is not a choice for ordinary code.

questions.prompt: Where does a `CoroutineExceptionHandler` actually take effect?
options: On root coroutines, such as a launch directly in the scope
questions.explanation: An exception travels up to the root before anything handles it, so a handler installed on a child is never consulted — the failure has already gone past it. It has to be on the root coroutine, or on the scope itself.
whyWrong: On a child it is quietly ignored, which is why people think it does not work.
With `async` it is different again: the exception is kept and thrown by `await()`.
It works in any scope. `runBlocking` has nothing to do with it.

questions.prompt: Why can a calculation loop keep running after `job.cancel()`?
options: Cancellation is cooperative: you have to check with isActive or ensureActive()
You have to call join() first
questions.explanation: `cancel()` raises a flag; it does not interrupt anything. All the suspending functions check the flag, which is why cancellation normally just works. A loop that suspends nowhere never checks, so it carries on.
whyWrong: The dispatcher has nothing to do with it: the flag is raised the same way everywhere.
`join()` waits for it to finish, which is a different thing from asking it to stop.
They can, as soon as they check — one call to `ensureActive()` is enough.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this code?
options: It swallows the CancellationException and carries on
questions.explanation: Cancellation arrives as a `CancellationException`, and `catch (e: Exception)` catches it. So when somebody cancels this coroutine, the exception is logged and `doMoreWork()` runs anyway — the cancellation has been quietly ignored. Rethrow it, or catch only what you expect.
whyWrong: There is a real bug: the coroutine cannot be cancelled while this `catch` is there.
`delay` throws exactly that exception when cancelled: that is how cancellation gets out.
`log` is not the problem here; the swallowed cancellation is.

questions.prompt: How is `viewModelScope` configured?
questions.explanation: `SupervisorJob` so that one failing coroutine does not cancel the others in the same ViewModel, and `Main.immediate` so updating the state does not even cost a hop when you are already on the main thread. Everything is cancelled when the ViewModel goes.
whyWrong: It starts on Main, not IO: a repository moves to IO itself when it needs to.
`Default` is for calculation, and a plain `Job` would mean one failure cancels everything.
`GlobalScope` has no parent and is never cancelled, which is the opposite of what a ViewModel scope is for.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between `coroutineScope` and `supervisorScope`?
options: supervisorScope does not wait for its children
In supervisorScope a failing child does not cancel the others
questions.explanation: Both wait for their children. The difference is what a failure does: in a plain scope it cancels the siblings, which is right when you need all the results; in a supervisor scope the siblings carry on, which is right when the parts are independent.
whyWrong: It does wait: that is part of structured concurrency in both.
Neither creates a thread. That is the dispatcher's job.
They really are different, and picking the wrong one is a real bug.

questions.prompt: Where can you call a `suspend` function from?
options: From a coroutine, or from another suspend function
questions.explanation: A suspending function needs somewhere that knows how to pause and resume it, and only a coroutine provides that. The compiler enforces the chain, so it is impossible to call one from a place that could not handle the pause.
whyWrong: From a normal function it does not compile, precisely because there would be no way to pause.
The thread is irrelevant: what matters is being inside a coroutine.
Any dispatcher is fine. The dispatcher decides which thread, not whether you are allowed.

questions.prompt: An `async` inside a `coroutineScope` fails. What happens?
options: The failure cancels the scope straight away, and await() rethrows it
It only surfaces when you call await()
You need a handler to see it
questions.explanation: Inside a scope with a normal `Job`, a failure goes up to the parent immediately and cancels the siblings. The exception is also kept, so `await()` rethrows it — but by then the cancelling has already happened.
whyWrong: That is only true for an `async` started on a scope with a `SupervisorJob`, where the failure does not propagate.
Nothing is ignored: the scope is cancelled and the exception reaches the caller.
A handler is not consulted here. The exception comes out of `await()` or out of the scope.

topics.title: Flow: values that keep arriving
topics.summary: A suspend function gives you one value; a Flow gives you a stream of them over time. Cold and hot, StateFlow, and how to collect without leaking.

lesson.heading: One value, or many over time
lesson.body:
A `suspend` function produces **one** value and finishes. But plenty of things produce values over and over: what the user types, rows in a database that keep changing, a position from the GPS.

A **`Flow`** is that: a stream of values arriving over time, which you can transform and which knows how to stop.

The first thing to understand is that a flow is **cold**. Writing one does nothing at all — it is a recipe, not a running process. The code inside only starts when somebody **collects** it, and it starts again, from the beginning, for every collector. Two collectors mean two independent runs.

That is why `collect` is a `suspend` function: collecting means waiting for values, possibly forever, and that needs a coroutine.

And it is why a flow cancels cleanly: it is tied to the coroutine collecting it, so when that is cancelled, the producing code stops too. No listener to remove, nothing to forget.

lesson.heading: The operators, and where the work happens
lesson.body:
A flow is transformed like a collection: `map`, `filter`, `onEach`. But because values arrive over **time**, there are operators that only make sense here.

**`debounce(300)`** — wait for a pause before letting a value through. The classic use is a search box: do not query the server on every letter.
**`distinctUntilChanged()`** — drop a value identical to the one before.
**`flatMapLatest`** — when a new value arrives, **cancel the work started by the previous one** and start again. That is what makes a search feel right: the reply to "ab" is useless once the user has typed "abc".
**`combine`** — take the latest from two flows and produce something from both.
**`catch`** — handle an error from upstream, and usually emit something safe instead.

Then there is **`flowOn`**, which decides where the work runs. The rule is the one that gets asked: **`flowOn` affects everything above it in the chain, never below.** So you put it after the expensive operators and before the collector, which always runs where its coroutine is.

And a thing to avoid: do not use `withContext` inside a `flow { }` to change the thread. A flow has to emit from the context it was collected in, and doing that throws. `flowOn` is the way.

lesson.heading: StateFlow: a value that always exists
lesson.body:
A plain flow has no "current value": arrive late and you have missed everything. For the state of a screen that is no use — a screen rebuilt after rotation has to be able to ask "what is the state **now**?".

**`StateFlow`** is a flow that always holds exactly one value, the latest. It is **hot**: it exists and holds its value whether anyone is collecting or not, and a new collector immediately receives the current value and then the changes.

Three things that follow, and all three get asked:

**It needs an initial value**, because it must always have one.
**It drops equal values.** Assign a value that `equals` the current one and nothing is emitted. That is usually what you want, and it is why your state should be a `data class` — so the comparison is on the contents.
**It keeps only the latest.** A slow collector does not see every intermediate value, just the most recent. For state that is right; for events it is wrong, and that is what `SharedFlow` is for.

The usual shape in a ViewModel: a private `MutableStateFlow` you change, and a public read-only view of it, so the screen can read but not write.

lesson.heading: SharedFlow, and the five-second rule
lesson.body:
**`SharedFlow`** is the other hot flow: no current value, no initial value, no dropping of equal ones. It is for **events** rather than state — show a message, navigate away, play a sound. Things that happen once and must happen even if the same one happened a moment ago.

Its `replay` setting says how many past values a new collector receives. `replay = 0` is the right default for events: somebody arriving later should not be shown a message from five minutes ago.

**`stateIn`** and **`shareIn`** turn a cold flow into a hot one, so that ten collectors share one run instead of starting ten. They take a `SharingStarted`, and that is where the five seconds come from:

**`Eagerly`** — start at once and never stop. Wasteful.
**`Lazily`** — start at the first collector and never stop.
**`WhileSubscribed(5_000)`** — stop five seconds after the last collector goes.

The five seconds exist for one reason: a rotation destroys the screen and rebuilds it, which means the collector disappears and comes back about a second later. Without the delay the database query would be cancelled and immediately restarted, every single rotation. With it, the gap passes unnoticed. It is the default you want.

lesson.heading: Collecting without leaking
lesson.body:
On Android, collecting a flow in a screen has one trap: if the collection does not stop when the screen goes away, it carries on updating views that are no longer there — and starts again every time the user comes back, so after a few trips there are four collectors doing the same work.

The answer in views is **`repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)`**. It starts the collection when the screen becomes visible and **cancels** it when it stops being visible, and does that again every time. Plain `lifecycleScope.launch` is not enough: it only stops when the screen is destroyed, so a screen hidden behind another goes on collecting.

In Compose the same thing is **`collectAsStateWithLifecycle()`**, and the difference from plain `collectAsState()` is exactly this: the one with lifecycle stops below STARTED, the other does not.

And in a Fragment, remember the other half: use **`viewLifecycleOwner`**, not the fragment, because a fragment outlives its view.

One last comparison, because it is asked: **`StateFlow` against `LiveData`.** `LiveData` knows about the lifecycle on its own and does not need an initial value; `StateFlow` is pure Kotlin, has no Android dependency, needs an initial value, and needs you to collect it in a lifecycle-aware way. New code uses `StateFlow`; `LiveData` is still everywhere in existing code.

questions.prompt: When is "start" printed?
questions.explanation: A flow is cold: writing it builds a description and runs nothing. The body starts when somebody collects, and it starts again from the beginning for each collector — so with three collectors you see "start" three times.
whyWrong: Creating it only makes the object. Nothing inside has run.
Only on the first would mean the result was shared, which is what a hot flow does, not a cold one.
It is printed as soon as anyone collects.

questions.prompt: What happens when you give a `MutableStateFlow` a value equal to the one it already has?
options: Nothing is emitted: equal values are dropped
It is queued in a buffer
questions.explanation: `StateFlow` compares with `equals` and drops a value identical to the current one, which saves pointless redraws. It is also why your state should be a `data class` — otherwise the comparison is by identity and every copy counts as different.
whyWrong: Re-emitting is what a `SharedFlow` does, which is why events belong there.
Nothing throws: it is a normal assignment that quietly does nothing.
There is no buffer: a `StateFlow` only ever holds the latest value.

questions.prompt: Which one needs an initial value?
questions.explanation: A `StateFlow` must always have a current value, so it has to start with one — that is what lets a new collector get something immediately. A `SharedFlow` has no current value at all, so there is nothing to initialise.
whyWrong: A `SharedFlow` has no state to hold, so it cannot have an initial value.
Only one of the two holds a value.
`StateFlow` genuinely requires it: it does not compile without.

questions.prompt: Which part of the chain does `flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)` affect?
questions.explanation: `flowOn` changes the context of the **upstream** operators — the ones written before it. Everything after it, and the collector itself, stay in the context of the coroutine that is collecting. That is why you put it right after the expensive work.
whyWrong: It is the opposite: what comes after is untouched.
The collector always runs in its own coroutine's context, and no operator can change that.
Not the whole chain: that is exactly the point of it being directional.

questions.prompt: Why `SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000)`?
options: It keeps the source alive for 5 s after the last collector, so a rotation does not restart it
It delays the first value by 5 seconds
It is a timeout for the first value
questions.explanation: A rotation destroys the screen and rebuilds it: the collector disappears and comes back about a second later. Without the delay the database query would be cancelled and immediately restarted every time. Five seconds covers the gap comfortably.
whyWrong: Nothing is delayed: the first collector gets values at once.
It is not about waiting for a value; it is about how long to keep going without collectors.
Replay is a separate setting and is about how many past values a newcomer receives.

questions.prompt: What does `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` add over `collectAsState()`?
options: It stops collecting when the screen drops below STARTED
It turns the Flow into LiveData
questions.explanation: Plain `collectAsState` keeps collecting while the composable exists, even with the app in the background — doing work nobody can see, and draining the battery. The lifecycle version stops when the screen is no longer visible and starts again when it is.
whyWrong: Speed is not the difference: the difference is when it stops.
It works with any `Flow`. `LiveData` has its own `observeAsState`.
No conversion happens: it stays a `Flow`.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `map` first turns them into 10, 20, 30; then `filter` keeps what is above 10, which drops the 10 and leaves `[20, 30]`. The order of the operators matters: filtering first would have given something else.
whyWrong: That is after the map, before the filter ran.
The values were multiplied by ten: they are not the originals.
[30] would be what is above 20. The test is above 10.

questions.prompt: For a search that must cancel the previous request on every keystroke, which operator?
questions.explanation: `flatMapLatest` cancels the work started by the previous value as soon as a new one arrives. In a search that is exactly right: the results for "ab" are worthless once the user has typed "abc", and you avoid both the wasted request and the answers arriving out of order.
whyWrong: `flatMapConcat` waits for each to finish before starting the next, so every letter's search runs in full.
`flatMapMerge` runs them all at once and mixes the results, so an older answer can overwrite a newer one.
`zip` pairs up two flows element by element. It is a different thing entirely.

questions.prompt: What does a new collector receive immediately?
questions.code:
val shared = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(replay = 1)
shared.emit(1)
shared.emit(2)
// a new collector arrives
questions.explanation: `replay = 1` means the flow keeps the **last** value for whoever arrives later. The 1 has already been pushed out by the 2, so the newcomer gets 2 and then whatever comes next.
whyWrong: Nothing would be `replay = 0`, which is the usual choice for events.
Both would need `replay = 2`.
The 1 is the one that was discarded: replay keeps the most recent.

questions.prompt: Which comparison between LiveData and StateFlow is right?
options: LiveData is cold, StateFlow is hot
StateFlow knows about the lifecycle on its own
StateFlow needs an initial value, LiveData does not
questions.explanation: A `StateFlow` must always have a current value, so you have to give it one. `LiveData` can be created empty and simply emits nothing until something is set. It is one of the practical differences when porting old code.
whyWrong: Both are hot: both hold a value independently of who is listening.
It does not, and that is the main thing you have to supply yourself — with `repeatOnLifecycle` or `collectAsStateWithLifecycle`.
It is the other way round: `StateFlow` drops equal values, `LiveData` emits them again.

topics.title: Compose and how to organise an app
topics.summary: Describing the interface instead of changing it, where the state has to live, the effects that are not the interface, and how the layers of an app fit together.

lesson.heading: Describing instead of changing
lesson.body:
With the old Android views you found the view and changed it: `textView.text = "hello"`. The interface was a thing you kept in sync, by hand, every time something changed. Forget one place and the screen is wrong.

**Compose** turns it round. You write a function that says **what the screen looks like for a given state**, and when the state changes, Compose calls that function again and updates what is different. You never touch a view.

Running it again is called **recomposition**, and it is cleverer than it sounds: only the parts that actually depend on what changed are re-run. The rest is skipped.

Three consequences that follow directly, and they explain most of the beginner mistakes:

**A composable can run many times, in any order, even in parallel.** So it must not have side effects: no network calls, no writing to a variable outside, no logging a visit. Those belong in the effects, below.

**A normal variable is useless.** Set `var count = 0` inside a composable and every recomposition starts it at 0 again. State has to be held in something Compose knows about.

**The order in which composables run is not guaranteed.** Anything that relies on "this one runs before that one" is wrong.

lesson.heading: remember, rememberSaveable, and what survives what
lesson.body:
**`mutableStateOf`** creates a value Compose watches: change it and whatever read it is re-run.

**`remember`** keeps that value across recompositions. Without it a new one would be created each time and nothing would ever change.

**`rememberSaveable`** also survives a **rotation**, because it writes the value into the same bundle the system restores. It only works with things that can be saved — numbers, text, anything parcelable — or with a saver you write.

The ladder of what survives what is the thing to know, and it is three steps:

**`remember`** — survives recomposition. Gone on rotation.
**`rememberSaveable`** — survives rotation. Gone on process death unless the state is small and saveable.
**`ViewModel` + `SavedStateHandle`** — survives rotation, and the `SavedStateHandle` part survives process death too.

So: `remember` for something that belongs to the interface — whether a menu is open, an animation's progress. A `ViewModel` for the data and the real state of the screen. And `rememberSaveable` for the small interface things that would be annoying to lose, like which tab was selected.

lesson.heading: State hoisting: one direction only
lesson.body:
A composable holding its own state cannot be controlled from outside, cannot be tested with a given value, and cannot be reused anywhere that needs the value elsewhere.

**State hoisting** means moving the state up to whoever uses the composable, and giving the composable two things instead: **the value to show**, and **a function to call when the user does something**.

That makes it **stateless**: it holds nothing, it decides nothing, it just draws what it is given and reports what happened. Those are the easy ones to test, to preview and to reuse.

The pattern this produces is **unidirectional data flow**, and it is the backbone of a Compose app: state goes **down** from the ViewModel to the composables, events go **up** from the composables to the ViewModel, and nothing goes sideways.

The rule for how far up to lift it: **to the lowest common ancestor of everyone who needs it**. No higher — pushing everything to the top makes the whole screen recompose for a change only one field cares about.

lesson.heading: Effects: everything that is not drawing
lesson.body:
A composable must only describe the interface. But sometimes you need to do something else: start a download, register a listener, show a message. Those are **side effects**, and they have their own functions so that they happen a controlled number of times.

**`LaunchedEffect(key)`** — runs a coroutine when the composable enters, cancels it when it leaves, and **starts over if the key changes**. For loading data, for an animation, for showing a snackbar. `LaunchedEffect(Unit)` means "once, on entry".

**`DisposableEffect(key)`** — the same shape, but with a mandatory `onDispose`. For anything that has to be undone: adding a listener, registering an observer. If you register something without this, you leak.

**`SideEffect`** — runs after every successful recomposition. For telling something non-Compose about the current state.

**`derivedStateOf`** — for when a value changes often but what you work out from it rarely does. The classic case is "is the list scrolled past the first item": the scroll position changes with every pixel, the true-or-false changes once. Without it everything recomposes on every pixel.

**`rememberUpdatedState`** — for a long-lived effect that has to use the latest version of a callback without restarting.

lesson.heading: The layers of an app
lesson.body:
Above individual screens, the shape nearly every Android app settles on is three layers, with the dependencies all pointing the same way.

**UI** — composables and ViewModel. Shows the state, reports events.
**Domain** — the business rules, usually as use cases. Pure Kotlin, no Android anywhere.
**Data** — repositories, network, database. It decides where things come from and hides that from everyone above.

The rule that makes it worth doing: **UI and data both depend on the domain, and the domain depends on nothing.** So the rules can be tested in milliseconds with no device, and you can change the database or the whole interface without touching them.

**MVVM against MVI**: MVVM has several pieces of state that the view puts together; MVI has **one immutable state object**, and events are reduced into a new one. MVI costs a little more ceremony and gives you one thing that matters at scale — at any moment there is a single value that describes the whole screen, which makes bugs reproducible and the history inspectable.

**Hilt** is the dependency injection: it builds objects and hands them to whoever needs them, so a class asks for what it wants in its constructor instead of creating it. That is what makes it possible to pass a fake repository in a test.

questions.prompt: After a rotation, a value held in `remember { mutableStateOf(0) }`:
options: Goes back to its starting value
questions.explanation: `remember` only survives recomposition, and a rotation destroys and rebuilds the whole screen. For it to survive you need `rememberSaveable`, which writes the value into the bundle the system restores — or a ViewModel for anything bigger.
whyWrong: Keeping it would need `rememberSaveable` or a ViewModel.
Nothing throws: the composition simply starts again from the beginning.
`remember` and the ViewModel are separate things: it does not put anything there.

questions.prompt: What happens when you tap the button?
options: The text updates on every tap
questions.explanation: Two things are wrong at once. The variable is not state Compose watches, so changing it triggers no recomposition; and even if something else caused one, `count = 0` would run again and reset it. It needs `remember { mutableIntStateOf(0) }`.
whyWrong: For it to update, the value would have to be state Compose is watching.
It compiles perfectly, which is what makes the mistake so easy to make.
Nothing crashes: it just silently never updates.

questions.prompt: When does a `LaunchedEffect(Unit)` block run?
options: Once when it enters the composition, and is cancelled when it leaves
questions.explanation: The key decides when it starts again. `Unit` never changes, so it runs once on entry and is cancelled when the composable leaves. Passing a real key — an id, for instance — makes it start over when that key changes.
whyWrong: Running on every recomposition is exactly what it exists to prevent: a composable can be re-run dozens of times.
Process death has nothing to do with it.
The coroutine runs in the composition's own scope, not on a special thread. Where it does its work is up to the dispatcher.

questions.prompt: What does "state hoisting" mean?
options: Moving the state up to the caller and passing a value and a callback
Putting all the state in remember
questions.explanation: The composable stops holding anything: it is given the value to show and a function to call when something happens. That makes it easy to test, easy to preview and reusable, and it is what produces one-way data flow.
whyWrong: Saving to disk is persistence, which is a different problem.
Globals are the opposite: the state would be shared by everybody.
Putting more in `remember` keeps the state inside, which is the thing hoisting is moving away from.

questions.prompt: Which effect do you use to register a listener and remove it when the composable leaves?
questions.explanation: `DisposableEffect` is the only one with a compulsory `onDispose`, which is called when the composable leaves or the key changes. That is exactly where you remove the listener. Without it, every visit to the screen adds one more and never removes it.
whyWrong: `LaunchedEffect` cancels its coroutine, but it has no place to undo a registration.
`SideEffect` runs after a recomposition and has no cleanup at all.
`derivedStateOf` is about computing a value, not about effects.

questions.prompt: When is `derivedStateOf` worth using?
options: To save state in the bundle
When a state changes often but what you work out from it rarely does
questions.explanation: The classic case is "is the list scrolled past the first item". The scroll position changes with every pixel; the true-or-false changes once. Without `derivedStateOf`, everything that reads it recomposes on every pixel.
whyWrong: That is `LaunchedEffect`.
That is `rememberSaveable`.
That is Hilt, and nothing to do with Compose state.

questions.prompt: How do you make a ViewModel injectable with Hilt?
options: Only with a module of its own
questions.explanation: The two together tell Hilt how to build it and let `hiltViewModel()` find it. A ViewModel cannot be a plain injectable object, because the framework has to create it through its own factory and tie it to the screen's lifetime.
whyWrong: `@AndroidEntryPoint` goes on the Activity or Fragment, not on the ViewModel.
A module is for binding an interface to an implementation. The ViewModel itself only needs the annotation.
`@Singleton` would make it live for the whole app, which is the opposite of what a ViewModel is for.

questions.prompt: What sets MVI apart from MVVM?
options: One immutable state, with events reduced into a new state
questions.explanation: In MVVM a screen can have several independent pieces of state, and the view puts them together. In MVI there is exactly one object describing the whole screen, and every event produces a new one. That makes a bug reproducible: you have the single value that caused it.
whyWrong: It uses them: the ViewModel is where the state and the reduction live.
It works just as well with Flow. The pattern has nothing to do with the library.
The data layer stays exactly where it was: MVI is about how the UI is organised.

questions.prompt: In Clean Architecture, which way do the dependencies point?
options: The domain depends on the data layer
The data layer depends on the UI
UI and data depend on the domain; the domain depends on nothing
questions.explanation: The rules sit at the centre and know nothing about the database or the screen. That is what lets you test them with no device, and change the database or the whole interface without touching them. The interface for a repository lives in the domain; the implementation lives in the data layer.
whyWrong: That would be the wrong way round, and the rules would then depend on the database.
The data layer must not know the UI exists.
Hilt is a tool for wiring things together. The layers depend on each other, not on it.

questions.prompt: With Strong Skipping on, how is an unstable parameter treated?
options: It always makes the composable non-skippable
It is compared by identity, so skipping is still possible
questions.explanation: Before Strong Skipping, a single unstable parameter — a plain `List`, a lambda — meant the composable could never be skipped and recomposed every time. Now it is compared by identity, so if it is literally the same object the composable is skipped. That is why using immutable types and `remember` for lambdas still pays off.
whyWrong: That was the behaviour before Strong Skipping, and it was the reason for a lot of needless recomposition.
`equals` is used for stable types. Unstable ones are compared by identity.
It compiles: nothing about stability is an error.
